title: Russian Doll Envelopes
description:
# Russian Doll Envelopes

You are given a 2D integer array `envelopes`, where `envelopes[i] = [wi, hi]` represents the width and height of the `i`th envelope.

One envelope can fit into another envelope if and only if both its width and height are strictly smaller than the other envelope's width and height.

Return the maximum number of envelopes you can nest one inside another.

You cannot rotate an envelope.

## Example 1:

**Input:** envelopes = [[5,4],[6,4],[6,7],[2,3]]

**Output:** 3

**Explanation:** One optimal chain is [2,3] -> [5,4] -> [6,7]. The two width-6 envelopes cannot contain each other because widths must be strictly different.

## Example 2:

**Input:** envelopes = [[1,1],[1,1],[1,1]]

**Output:** 1

**Explanation:** Equal envelopes cannot be nested because both dimensions must be strictly larger.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= envelopes.length <= 10^5`
* `envelopes[i].length == 2`
* `1 <= wi, hi <= 10^5`

solutions.name: Sort and Height LIS with Binary Search
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort envelopes by width ascending. For equal widths, sort height descending. After that ordering, run the classic patience-sorting Longest Increasing Subsequence algorithm on the heights.

## Key Insight

The descending tie-break is the whole trick. It prevents two envelopes with the same width from appearing as an increasing height subsequence, so a strict LIS on heights now represents a valid two-dimensional nesting chain.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Quadratic Chain Dynamic Programming
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort by width ascending and height ascending, then let `dp[i]` be the longest valid chain ending at envelope `i`. Check every earlier envelope and extend only when both width and height are strictly smaller.

## Key Insight

This baseline keeps the original two-dimensional rule visible. It is too slow for the largest constraint, but it is the clearest correctness model for why both dimensions, not just height, must be checked.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Fenwick Tree Maximum DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort by width ascending and equal-width height descending, then coordinate-compress heights. A Fenwick tree stores the best chain length ending at each compressed height prefix. For every envelope, query strictly smaller heights and update its own height.

## Key Insight

After the same-width descending tie-break, every processed envelope has width no greater than the current one, and the height prefix query excludes equal or taller envelopes. The data structure computes the same recurrence as LIS while exposing it as range maximum DP.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Segment Tree Maximum DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the same width ordering and height compression as the Fenwick route, but keep maximum chain lengths in an iterative segment tree. Query the range of ranks strictly below the current height and point-update the current height with the new chain length.

## Key Insight

The segment tree makes the DP interval explicit: every valid predecessor must have a smaller height rank. This route is useful when the range aggregate later needs to be changed or extended beyond a simple prefix maximum.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Width-Grouped Fenwick DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort by width ascending and height ascending, then process all envelopes with the same width as one batch. Compute each batch member's best value from previously completed widths first, and only then write the batch updates into a Fenwick tree.

## Key Insight

Batching is another way to enforce the strict width rule. Envelopes with equal width are never allowed to feed one another, so delaying their updates until the whole width group has been queried prevents accidental same-width chains without needing the descending height tie-break.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
